title: Tetralogy of Fallot
summary: Why one outflow obstruction explains the blue baby, the murmur, the spells, the boot and the surgery.
closing: Remember the one idea that ties it all together: the tighter the RVOT, the bluer the child. Echo confirms it, knee-chest buys time in a spell, and surgery fixes it.

objectives.text: State that TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease and that it most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.
Name the four components of classic TOF, identify ASD, PDA and LVH as not among them, and define pentalogy of Fallot.
Explain how the degree of RVOT obstruction sets the direction of shunting, the degree of cyanosis, pulmonary oligaemia and the 'pink Tet'.
Describe the TOF murmur and S2, and why the murmur softens during a tet spell.
Interpret the ECG and chest X-ray of TOF and choose echocardiography as the gold standard, with CT and MRI as adjuncts.
Recognise the triggers of a tet (hypercyanotic) spell and manage it step by step, giving the reason for each step.
Outline surgical management: debated timing of complete repair, the Blalock-Taussig shunt as palliation, and pulmonary valve replacement after repair.
List the long-term problems after repair: pulmonary regurgitation (the commonest indication for reoperation), ventricular arrhythmias and late sudden death.
State the causes of death and complications of unrepaired TOF, and the lifelong endocarditis risk.
Know the associations and epidemiology of TOF (right aortic arch, 22q11.2 deletion, incidence), and that sources differ on the numbers.
Answer the PYQ keys where they differ from current sources: 'most common cyanotic CHD beyond the neonatal period' and the boot-shaped heart in infants.
Go deeper on surgical strategy and imaging limits: who gets staged palliation, ideal repair window, shunt drawbacks, and pulmonary artery assessment.

misconceptions.text: An atrial septal defect is one of the four components of TOF.
misconceptions.source: P1 (pattern: RUHS 2022 'not part of TOF' key) and Exam note K77

misconceptions.text: A patent ductus arteriosus is one of the four components of TOF.
misconceptions.source: P1 (pattern: AIIMS Patna 2020 'not part of TOF' key) and Exam note K77

misconceptions.text: TOF causes left ventricular hypertrophy (the hypertrophied ventricle is the left one).
misconceptions.source: P1 (pattern: multi-select distractor LVH) and Exam note K77

misconceptions.text: Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus a PDA (or plus some fifth lesion other than an ASD).
Every TOF baby is deeply blue, and how blue they are depends on the size of the VSD.
misconceptions.source: Predictable wrong model (attributing cyanosis to the hole, not the obstruction)

misconceptions.text: The murmur comes from flow across the VSD, so it gets louder during a tet spell as more blood shunts right to left.
misconceptions.source: Predictable wrong model (reversed mechanism; brief: murmur origin)

misconceptions.text: In a tet spell you should lower systemic resistance (vasodilate) or treat it like heart failure with a diuretic.
misconceptions.source: Predictable wrong model (reversing the SVR logic)

misconceptions.text: The boot-shaped heart means the heart is enlarged (cardiomegaly).
misconceptions.source: P3 (pattern) — predictable wrong model of the X-ray sign

misconceptions.text: The boot-shaped chest X-ray (or ECG) is the investigation of choice that confirms TOF.
misconceptions.source: P3 (pattern) over-generalised; look-alike 'classic sign' vs 'gold standard'

misconceptions.text: After TOF repair, the commonest reason to reoperate is a residual VSD or recurrent pulmonary stenosis.
misconceptions.source: Predictable wrong model (expecting the original lesions to recur)

segments.title: The blue baby with a loud murmur
segments.goal: Pose a NEET PG-style vignette of a cyanosed infant with a harsh ejection murmur that the learner tries to name and explain before any teaching.

prefer.reason: A case puts the curiosity gap (why blue, why that murmur) up front.

segments.title: Four parts, and what is not one of them
segments.goal: Have the learner recall the four components of TOF and reject ASD, PDA and LVH, with a fast lane for those who already know them.

prefer.reason: Most students have met the four components in anatomy; a retrieval gate lets them prove it and move on.

segments.title: It's the outflow, not the hole
segments.goal: Build the model that the degree of RVOT obstruction decides how much blood bypasses the lungs, and so the cyanosis, the oligaemia and the pink Tet.

prefer.reason: Predicting what happens to the shunt as the RVOT tightens is the core mental model.

segments.title: Listening to TOF and spotting a spell
segments.goal: Let the learner work out the murmur, the single S2 and the tet spell triggers from the mechanism, including why the murmur softens in a spell.

prefer.reason: The murmur fading in a spell is counter-intuitive; predict-then-explain exposes the wrong VSD model.

segments.title: ECG, the boot and the gold standard
segments.goal: Have the learner read the ECG and chest X-ray of TOF and choose echocardiography as the gold standard, with CT and MRI as adjuncts.

segments.title: Managing the spell, the repair and the years after
segments.goal: Walk a child through a tet spell, then through palliation, complete repair and life after repair, choosing each step and its reason.

prefer.reason: A spell is a time-pressured decision; a case makes each step a choice with a reason.

segments.title: Exam traps
segments.goal: Drill the PYQ stems (components, 'not part of TOF', pentalogy, boot-shaped heart, most common cyanotic CHD) and teach both the PYQ key and the current source where they differ.

prefer.reason: P1–P4 supply real keyed stems and distractors.

segments.title: Build your TOF one-pager
segments.goal: The learner assembles the take-home summary (true statements, spell steps in order, the high-yield 'most commons') and leaves with review cards.

prefer.reason: Ordering the spell steps and picking the 'most commons' is the natural summary.
